clinicalPearls: Familial isolated hyperparathyroidism is a diagnosis of exclusion: hereditary primary hyperparathyroidism in two or more relatives without the extra-parathyroid features of MEN1, MEN2A or the hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome.
Inheritance is autosomal dominant and the disorder is genetically heterogeneous, with germline variants described in MEN1, CDC73 and CASR and activating variants in GCM2.
Some kindreds are incomplete or early expressions of MEN1 or the hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome that only declare themselves years later, so lifelong surveillance is essential.
GCM2 gain-of-function variants are an increasingly recognised cause and may be associated with multiglandular and more aggressive disease.
CDC73 (HRPT2) carriers have a meaningfully increased risk of atypical parathyroid tumours and parathyroid carcinoma, warranting heightened vigilance.
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia must be excluded using the urinary calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio, as it mimics the biochemistry but does not benefit from parathyroidectomy.
Multiglandular hyperplasia is common, so pre-operative localisation and often bilateral neck assessment are important to avoid persistent disease.
Germline genetic testing clarifies the underlying gene and guides the extent of surgery, tumour surveillance and cascade screening of relatives.
reference.pathophysiology: Familial isolated hyperparathyroidism reflects an inherited predisposition to autonomous parathyroid hormone secretion in the absence of syndromic features. It is genetically heterogeneous: loss-of-function germline variants in the tumour-suppressor genes MEN1 (menin) and CDC73 (parafibromin) remove a brake on parathyroid cell proliferation, inactivating variants in CASR (the calcium-sensing receptor) reset the calcium set-point, and gain-of-function variants in GCM2, a transcription factor essential for parathyroid development, drive parathyroid growth. In the tumour-suppressor forms a somatic second hit produces an adenoma or hyperplasia with unregulated parathyroid hormone release, causing hypercalcaemia, hypophosphataemia and increased bone turnover and renal calcium handling. Because several of these genes also underlie recognised syndromes, apparently isolated familial disease may represent an allelic or incompletely penetrant variant of MEN1 or the hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome, which has direct implications for carcinoma risk and long-term surveillance.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (with pituitary and enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours)
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (with medullary thyroid carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma)
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (CASR, GNA11 or AP2S1 variants)
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease
Neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism from biallelic CASR inactivation
additionalInvestigations: Corrected serum calcium, ionised calcium and parathyroid hormone
Twenty-four-hour urinary calcium with the calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio to exclude familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
Serum phosphate, magnesium, vitamin D status and renal function
Neck ultrasound with sestamibi scintigraphy or four-dimensional CT for localisation
Bone densitometry with attention to cortical sites such as the distal radius
Renal imaging for nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis
Germline genetic testing panel covering MEN1, CDC73, CASR and GCM2
redFlags: Very high calcium with a firm or palpable neck mass suggesting parathyroid carcinoma, particularly in CDC73 carriers
Features suggesting an undisclosed multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome, such as pituitary, pancreatic or medullary thyroid disease
Severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia with confusion, dehydration or cardiac disturbance
Fragility fractures or progressive metabolic bone disease
Recurrent renal calculi or declining renal function
reference.prognosis: With appropriate parathyroidectomy and lifelong biochemical surveillance the outlook is generally good; it is less favourable in CDC73-related disease because of the risk of parathyroid carcinoma, persistent disease and recurrence.
pitfalls: Mislabelling familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia as familial isolated hyperparathyroidism and performing a futile parathyroidectomy
Assuming single-gland disease and missing multiglandular hyperplasia, leading to persistent or recurrent hypercalcaemia
Failing to test for CDC73 and thereby underestimating parathyroid carcinoma risk
Prematurely discharging patients when the condition may be an evolving MEN1 or hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome
Neglecting cascade genetic testing and biochemical screening of at-risk relatives
references: Clinical genetics references on hereditary hyperparathyroidism
Consensus guidelines on the management of primary hyperparathyroidism
management: Perform parathyroidectomy for symptomatic or biochemically significant primary hyperparathyroidism, using bilateral neck exploration given the frequency of multiglandular disease
Adopt a more extensive resection and heightened vigilance for parathyroid carcinoma in CDC73 (HRPT2) carriers
Control hypercalcaemia medically when surgery is deferred with a calcimimetic (cinacalcet) and a bisphosphonate for bone protection
Exclude familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia using the calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio before operating
Maintain lifelong biochemical surveillance of calcium and parathyroid hormone for persistent, recurrent or late-declaring MEN1 or hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour features
Assess complications with bone densitometry at cortical sites and renal imaging for nephrolithiasis
Undertake genetic testing of MEN1, CDC73, CASR and GCM2 with counselling and cascade screening of relatives
